entities.name: Alessandro Mattei
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alessandro Mattei (1744-1820) emerged as a pivotal figure in the Roman Curia during the tumultuous late 18th and early 19th centuries, a period defined by the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Wars. Born into the ancient and influential House of Mattei, a scion of the Roman aristocracy, his ecclesiastical career culminated in his elevation to Cardinal in 1794. Mattei's significance lies in his deep involvement in the Holy See's attempts to navigate the existential threats posed by revolutionary France and Napoleon Bonaparte, particularly as a negotiator and a symbol of papal resistance and resilience. He represented the traditionalist wing of the Church, striving to preserve papal sovereignty and the temporal power amidst unprecedented secularizing pressures that challenged the very foundations of the Papal States and Catholic Europe.

Mattei's career was marked by several critical diplomatic engagements. Following the French occupation of Rome in 1798 and the proclamation of the Roman Republic, he was among the cardinals exiled by General Louis-Alexandre Berthier, a direct consequence of Pope Pius VI's refusal to renounce temporal power. Mattei was instrumental in the conclave held in Venice in 1799-1800, which elected Pope Pius VII, a critical event for the survival of the papacy. Later, as Cardinal-Bishop of Palestrina, he became a central figure in the negotiations surrounding the Concordat of 1801 between Napoleon and Pius VII, a landmark agreement that re-established the Catholic Church in France after a decade of revolutionary upheaval, though not without significant concessions. His steadfast loyalty to the Pope saw him again exiled to France by Napoleon in 1809, alongside Pius VII, after the annexation of the Papal States.
